LoloBuy QC photo checklist: approve, question, or hold?

A practical method for comparing warehouse photos with the item you ordered. It helps you find visible mismatches before parcel submission without treating a photo as proof of fit, function, authenticity or future performance.

Editorial note: This independent guide is based on LoloBuy’s public purchase, standard-photo, standard-inspection and inspection-scope materials, checked on 20 September 2026. Service options and rules can change, so confirm the current order screen before making a warehouse decision.

What a LoloBuy QC photo can—and cannot—answer

A warehouse photo is most useful when it answers a question you defined before the item arrived. Does the visible product match the selected colour? Is the marked size the one you ordered? Is the quantity complete? Is an obvious accessory missing? Is there visible damage that would make you stop? Those are concrete comparisons. “Does this look good?” is not.

LoloBuy’s current public standard-inspection description says that its standard process checks appearance information such as style, quantity, colour, size and model, as well as visible damage or defects. It also says that the standard service provides three to six inspection photos before the item is repackaged and stocked. This defines a useful but limited evidence set: it can show what the warehouse received from several angles, but it is not an unlimited product test.

The same public rules describe important exclusions. Sealed products and many items with sealing labels are not opened; the check may be limited to the packaging and visible product information. Professional electronics, digital products and related accessories are outside the normal scope for authenticity, functionality and quality checks. A photo also cannot establish long-term durability, exact fit on your body or compliance with every US or European destination rule.

Your goal is therefore not to extract certainty from a few images. It is to decide whether the visible evidence is consistent enough with your saved order to continue, whether one precise question could resolve a gap, or whether a material mismatch should keep the item out of an international parcel.

Prepare the comparison before opening the photos

Do not begin with the warehouse gallery. Begin with the record of what you meant to buy. Open the saved listing or order details and write down five points: the original option label, colour or version, size or model, quantity, and included components that were explicitly stated. Add one or two “stop conditions”—details that would change your decision if they were wrong.

For clothing, a stop condition might be the wrong marked size, wrong colourway or missing belt. For shoes, it might be the wrong size label, a left/right mismatch or damage to the upper. For an accessory, it could be the wrong connector or width. Only use an included item as a stop condition if the seller’s listing or selected bundle actually promised it. Props shown in promotional photographs are not automatically part of the order.

This preparation matters because the QC set should be judged against the purchased specification, not against a memory of the main image. A listing may contain several batches, colours or bundles that share photographs. If you cannot identify your own selection, pause and recover the order record before approving anything.

Use a three-pass QC photo review

Pass 1: identity and option match

Start wide. Compare the overall style, silhouette, colour family and obvious design details with the selected option. Then look for the visible size tag, model label or package label. Count the units, pairs and components that can reasonably be seen. If you ordered a set, distinguish between a complete set and a single piece photographed from multiple angles.

Do not reject an item solely because warehouse lighting makes a colour appear warmer or cooler. Compare multiple frames, including any label or option sticker. But do not explain away a clearly different colourway, model or marked size. Record the image number and the exact mismatch rather than writing “wrong item.”

Pass 2: visible condition

Next, examine the areas most likely to show handling or manufacturing problems: front and back surfaces, seams, edges, soles, corners, closures and exposed hardware. Look for stains, tears, scratches, broken parts, large deformations, missing pieces or a left/right inconsistency. Zoom can help, but remember that compression, reflections and shadows can resemble defects.

Use at least two views before deciding that a mark is physical. A bright streak on glossy material may be reflected light; a repeated mark in the same location across different angles is stronger evidence. If the issue remains unclear and would affect your choice, ask for one targeted view rather than requesting a new general photo set.

Pass 3: the detail that drives your decision

Finally, check the details you identified in advance. If garment dimensions matter, a size tag alone is not a measurement. If compatibility matters, an outer-box model label may be the only visible evidence for a sealed item, and that still does not prove the device works. If packaging matters, decide whether cosmetic box damage affects your goal or only presentation.

LoloBuy’s public scope statement emphasizes appearance verification. Use that boundary honestly. Standard photos may support “the package label shows the ordered model” but not “the electronics are functional.” They may support “the visible size tag matches” but not “the item will fit me.” Keeping the conclusion no broader than the evidence prevents a photograph from becoming a false guarantee.

Choose one of three warehouse decisions

Approve when the visible evidence matches the saved order

Approval is reasonable when the identifiable option, marked size or model, quantity and visible condition are consistent with the order, and no unresolved stop condition remains. This does not mean the item is risk-free. It means the available warehouse evidence has not shown a material visible mismatch.

Before approval, save the relevant image references and confirm that you are reviewing the correct order. Then move to parcel planning only when all items selected for that parcel have reached their own decision. “Stored in warehouse” is an inventory status, not a recommendation to ship immediately.

Question when one answer would change the outcome

Ask a question when the evidence is incomplete but the missing fact is observable. Make the request narrow: “Please show the size tag,” “Please photograph the connector side,” “Please show both shoes together,” or “Please place a tape flat across the chest from pit to pit.” State the unit and method for any measurement.

Avoid vague requests such as “check quality,” “take better photos” or “is it good?” They do not identify what must be verified. LoloBuy’s public standard-photo material says a secondary quality-inspection service may be available after warehousing when inspection was not selected earlier. Availability, scope and any charge should be checked in the live account rather than assumed from this guide.

Hold when the mismatch is material or the evidence cannot support the decision

Hold the item when the photos show a different option, wrong marked size, missing unit, obvious damage or another saved stop condition. Also hold when the listing was too vague to establish what should have arrived. LoloBuy’s inspection rules note that orders without real product information—such as invalid links, mosaic product pictures or ambiguous multi-purpose listings—can limit what the warehouse is able to match beyond visible damage or stains.

A hold is not automatically a refund or return approval. It simply means you should not include the item in an international parcel until the current platform process, seller position and available remedy are clear. Keep the message factual: identify the selected option, cite the visible photo, and describe the difference in one sentence.

Apply stricter limits to sealed goods and electronics

For a sealed product, decide whether preserving the seal matters more than inspecting the contents. The published inspection rules say that many sealed non-clothing, non-bag and non-shoe products are not opened. In that situation, you may be able to compare the package condition, label and model, but not the contents or internal condition. Do not request an opened inspection without understanding that it could alter packaging or seller-return options.

For electronics, check externally visible compatibility information such as model, connector, plug marking or stated voltage when it appears in the photographs. Do not infer authenticity, battery health, full functionality or regional compliance from appearance. US and European buyers should separately confirm destination requirements and whether a chosen shipping route accepts the item category before parcel submission.

A repeatable checklist before international shipping

Use the same sequence for every item: recover the exact order selection; review identity and quantity; inspect visible condition; check the one or two details that matter most; write down any limitation; then mark the item “approve,” “question” or “hold.” If you ask for more evidence, decide in advance what answer would lead to approval and what answer would stop the item.

This method keeps QC review proportional. A basic garment may need a colour, tag, quantity and condition check. A fragile set may need component count and close-ups of vulnerable areas. A sealed electronic product may never produce enough warehouse evidence to prove function, so the decision must acknowledge that residual risk.

Conclusion: use photos as evidence, not reassurance

The useful LoloBuy QC photo checklist is evidence-led: compare the actual selection, inspect visible condition, respect the published inspection limits, and ask only for information that can change your decision. Approve when the visible facts line up, question when one observable detail is missing, and hold when a material mismatch remains. That discipline is more valuable than trying to make a small photo set answer questions it was never designed to prove.
